notes:
Need to search first.These notes cover 1 Kings 8:1–22, but the research ran short. My search and fetch tools hit their usage limit partway through, so most notes come from Enduring Word (David Guzik), Ellicott, Gill, the Pulpit Commentary and the shorter commentaries that biblehub and studylight show on the same pages. I left out anything I couldn't find. The gaps are listed at the end.

**v. 1**
- Guzik sees this as a grand opening ceremony. The temple couldn't start operating until the ark, its most important item, was in the Most Holy Place. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-8/
- Ellicott thinks the "elders" may be officials of the royal court, such as princes and counsellors, and the "heads of the tribes" the chiefs of the leading families. Only these were formally summoned. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/8.htm
- Gill notes that David had brought the ark to the fortress of Zion. Solomon now moved it up to Moriah, a higher hill close by. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-8.html

**v. 2**
- Ellicott: Ethanim was later called Tisri and falls in late September to early October. The name may mean "month of gifts," because of the harvest. The feast was Tabernacles, the most joyful feast of the year, which recalled the wilderness tents. It suited the moment, since the ark was moving from a tent to a permanent house. This time the festival ran fourteen days instead of seven (v. 65). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/8.htm
- Guzik: the temple was finished in the eighth month (6:38), so the dedication waited eleven months. He quotes Poole, who says the timing suited the people, since the harvest was in and they had already come for Tabernacles. He also quotes Clarke, who cites Archbishop Ussher's view that it was a jubilee year. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-8/
- **A different reading:** Gill says "the feast" was the dedication feast, not Tabernacles. It came first, and the two feasts together lasted fourteen days. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/8.htm

**v. 3**
- Guzik: Solomon was careful to have the ark carried only by priests. He didn't repeat David's mistake in 2 Samuel 6. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-8/
- Ellicott: carrying the ark on a journey was normally the job of the Kohathite Levites. Only priests could remove it from the inner sanctuary or put it back. That explains the careful wording in vv. 3, 4 and 6. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/8.htm
- Matthew Henry: since this was the ark's last journey, the priests carried it themselves. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_008.cfm

**v. 4**
- Ellicott: the Tent of Meeting was still at Gibeon. The priests and Levites had been split between it and the smaller tent on Zion. He suggests each group probably brought up what was in its charge, following the order in Numbers 3. We aren't told what became of the old tabernacle. It was probably stored in the temple precincts. He mentions the Jewish tradition in 2 Maccabees 2 that Jeremiah later hid it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/8.htm
- Guzik quotes Clarke: there were two tabernacles, one at Gibeon and the temporary tent David made on Zion. The lampstand, the bread table and the incense altar were also brought into the temple. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-8/
- Gill: the priests carried the ark and the Levites carried the vessels. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-8.html

**v. 5**
- Ellicott: this is a much larger version of David's sacrifices when he brought the ark to Zion (2 Samuel 6:13). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/8.htm
- Gill: the sacrifices took place while the ark was still in the priests' court. He reads "could not be counted" as deliberate exaggeration meaning a huge number. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-8.html
- Guzik: Solomon went far beyond what custom expected. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-8/
- Matthew Henry: the sacrifices honoured the ark and expressed joy that it had a settled home. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/8-8.html

**vv. 6–7**
- Gill: the cherubim's wings stretched from wall to wall and covered both the ark and its poles. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/8.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary says the ark would now always be in complete darkness under the wings. It thinks the evidence favours the ark lying north–south, in line with the wings. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-8.html

**v. 8 (the poles)**
- **Why they were pulled forward:**
  - Barnes, Ellicott and others: the law forbade removing the poles (Exodus 25:15). Pulling them forward showed that the ark had reached its resting place. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/8-8.htm and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/8.htm
  - Gill, Poole and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the poles guided the high priest to the ark in the dark on the Day of Atonement. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/8-8.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary rejects this guide idea as "mere conjecture." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-8.html
- **How they were seen:** the Cambridge Bible translates the verse as "the staves were long." The Rabbis said the pole ends pressed against the curtain as visible bulges; the Pulpit Commentary rejects this. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/8-8.htm
- **"To this day":**
  - Ellicott and Barnes say the phrase was copied from an older document written while the temple still stood. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/8.htm and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/8-8.htm
  - Ellicott adds that the Babylonian looting lists never mention the ark. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/8.htm
- **Devotional reading:** a preceptaustin page says the poles were no longer needed because the wilderness journey had ended. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64362/

**v. 9 (only the tablets; the main debated point)**
The question is how this fits with Hebrews 9:4, which places the manna jar and Aaron's rod inside the ark.
- **"Beside" the ark, not inside it.** Matthew Henry, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Poole, Benson and Gill read "in" in Hebrews as "by" or "near." Exodus and Numbers say the items were laid "before the testimony." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/8-9.htm and https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_008.cfm
  - Keil and Delitzsch go further. They think Hebrews follows a mistaken Jewish tradition about "before the testimony." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/8-9.htm
- **Once inside, later lost.**
  - The Pulpit Commentary suggests the Philistines took the items, perhaps the golden pot especially. It adds that "there was nothing" almost implies something had once been there. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/8-9.htm
  - The Geneva notes blame the ark's enemies. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/8-9.htm
  - Barnes (on Hebrews) blames the ark's journeys or its capture. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/9-4.html
  - A GotQuestions answer quoted on preceptaustin points to the men of Beth-shemesh who looked into the ark (1 Samuel 6:19). https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-8-commentary
  - Guzik simply says we don't know. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-8/
- **Carried inside, then moved.** The Cambridge Bible thinks the items were carried inside while the ark travelled and taken out once it reached the temple. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/8-9.htm
  - Coffman cites Canon Cook, who says Solomon moved them elsewhere. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/8-9.html
- **Trapp's note:** Trapp reports that Junius linked "in which" in Hebrews to the tabernacle, not to the ark. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/1-kings-8.html
- **Lessons drawn from the verse:**
  - Ellicott: keeping only the moral law in the ark ties religion and morality together. God is best known in his righteousness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/8.htm
  - Pulpit Homiletics: the covenant rested on law, and the mercy seat stood between people and the broken law. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_kings/8.htm
  - Jon Courson (quoted on preceptaustin): signs and wonders like the rod and the manna don't last, but the Word does. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-8-commentary
  - Kelly: only the law remained, and the wilderness comforts were gone. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/8-9.html
- **Guzik on the Exodus reference:** some 500 years later, this completes the Exodus. God's dwelling moves from a tent to a permanent building. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-8/

**vv. 10–11 (the cloud)**
- Ellicott: this is the Shekinah, the bright cloud of God's presence. It matches Sinai and the tabernacle's dedication (Exodus 40:34–35) and was a sign that God accepted the temple. Ezekiel later sees it leave (Ezekiel 10), and Haggai promises a greater glory. 2 Chronicles 5 says the cloud came as the Levites sang praise. The priests drew back out of awe more than terror, like Isaiah or the apostles at the Transfiguration. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/8.htm
- Guzik:
  - He traces the cloud through Scripture, all the way to the Transfiguration, the Ascension and Christ's return.
  - The priests couldn't continue because God is holy, which is not a "warm and fuzzy" feeling.
  - He quotes Patterson and Austel, who link this to Acts 2, where God marked the church as the Spirit's temple. This is the reading closest to a Pentecostal or charismatic one that I found.
  - He also says the New Covenant gives better access to God.
  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-8/
- Matthew Henry:
  - God showed his glory only after the priests came out. From then on, no one could approach the Most Holy Place casually. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/8-8.html
  - The cloud may also point to how dim that era was compared with the gospel's light. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/8-9.htm

**vv. 12–13**
- Ellicott: Solomon's words are broken and abrupt, out of awe. He is recalling Exodus 19:9 and Leviticus 16:2. "Thick darkness" doesn't contradict the glory, because too much light also darkens the eyes. It stands for the mystery of God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/8.htm
- **A scholarly proposal:** Thenius suggested changing "thick darkness" to "Jerusalem." Ellicott rejects this. The Septuagint, the Vulgate and Josephus all support the Hebrew wording, and the harder reading is the more likely original. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/8.htm
- Guzik: God did dwell in the temple in a special way, which was good as long as it didn't turn into superstition. He quotes Dilday, who says the poem seems incomplete and may have had another opening line. Later he adds that God is too great to be limited to the temple. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-8/

**v. 14**
- Ellicott: according to 2 Chronicles 6:13, Solomon stood on a bronze platform in the court. That let him turn between the temple and the people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/8.htm

**vv. 15–16**
- Ellicott: Solomon quotes God's promise in 2 Samuel 7 freely. On v. 16 he says the verse should be corrected from the fuller wording in 2 Chronicles 6:5–6 so it reads coherently. His comment breaks off at that point. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/8.htm
- Guzik: the temple fulfilled God's plan more than David's or Solomon's; they were his instruments. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-8/

**vv. 17–19**
- Ellicott: Solomon kindly leaves out the reason David was refused, his bloodshed (1 Chronicles 22:8; 28:3). He adds something the earlier accounts don't have: David "did well" to want to build. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/8.htm

**vv. 20–21**
- Guzik: Solomon keeps stressing the Exodus, which was still as real for Israel as when it happened. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-8/
- Gill: "the place" is the Most Holy Place. "The covenant" means the two tablets, as the Targum puts it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-8.html

**v. 22**
- Guzik:
  - Solomon prayed at the altar, not inside the temple, because he was a king and not a priest.
  - Spread hands were the usual Old Testament prayer posture, showing surrender and readiness to receive.
  - He quotes Spurgeon, who says the prayer reads like a summary of all future temple prayers and is full of language from the Pentateuch.
  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-8/

**What I couldn't find:**
- Pages from specific Protestant traditions (Reformed, Baptist, Lutheran, Methodist, Pentecostal) that disagree on these verses. The only real disagreements I found are among commentators: v. 2 (which feast), v. 8 (the poles) and v. 9 (Hebrews 9:4).
- Catholic and Orthodox readings (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org).
- NET Bible notes and Bible Odyssey articles.
- Any prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching on these verses.

A second round of searches, once the tools are available again, would be needed to fill these gaps.
